items.q: A 59-year-old man needs elective coronary angiography and asks to sit up and walk soon after. He has strong wrist pulses with no Raynaud symptoms and no fistula. The operator considers wrist access. Which pre-puncture check best confirms the hand will stay perfused if the radial artery occludes?
o: Barbeau plethysmography of ulnar collateral flow through the palmar arch
Measuring his shoe size for catheter length
Checking his blood group for radial suitability
Asking his star sign for procedural luck
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Barbeau plethysmography of ulnar collateral flow through the palmar arch.** The ulnar artery feeds the hand through the palmar arch when the radial blocks, and Barbeau testing proves that backup.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Shoe size never guides arterial access
- C: Blood groups ignore collateral circulation
- D: Star signs cannot protect hands
**Key point:** Barbeau testing confirms ulnar backup flow.
items.kp: Radial access needs proven ulnar collateral flow.

items.q: A 63-year-old woman undergoes transradial visceral embolisation and the catheter suddenly sticks midway with wrist pain. The artery grips the catheter firmly and the monitor shows no dissection flap. Which immediate response best manages this radial spasm with a stuck catheter?
o: Pause with vasodilators and sedation rather than forcing the catheter
Push harder until the catheter breaks through
Pull violently to strip the artery clean
Abandon the patient on the table at once
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Pause with vasodilators and sedation rather than forcing the catheter.** Spasm releases with relaxation and vasodilator drugs while force tears the small artery into dissection.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Force converts spasm into dissection
- C: Violent pulls avulse radial branches
- D: Abandonment helps neither spasm nor patient
**Key point:** Spasm needs pause with vasodilators, never force.
items.kp: Radial spasm demands pause with vasodilators, never force.

items.q: A 55-year-old man has his radial sheath removed after coronary work and a pressure band applied. The nurse keeps a pulse oximeter trace visible on the thumb during compression. Which haemostasis principle does maintaining thumb flow during band compression demonstrate?
o: Patent haemostasis keeping trickle flow to prevent radial occlusion
Tightest possible band to crush all flow
Removing the band within thirty seconds
Compressing the elbow instead of the wrist
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Patent haemostasis keeping trickle flow to prevent radial occlusion.** Keeping blood trickling through the radial during compression stops clot forming in a static column, cutting occlusion rates.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Crushing all flow invites occlusion
- C: Thirty seconds cannot seal arterial holes
- D: Elbow pressure misses the wrist hole
**Key point:** Patent haemostasis prevents radial occlusion.
items.kp: Radial bands use patent haemostasis with maintained flow.

items.q: A 48-year-old woman develops severe escalating forearm pain with a rock-tense forearm one hour after difficult transradial access with multiple punctures. Her fingers tingle and passive stretching hurts intensely. Which dreaded forearm complication does tense painful swelling with stretch pain suggest?
o: Compartment syndrome needing urgent surgical release
Mild bruising needing reassurance only
Contrast allergy of the forearm skin
Successful access with expected aching
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Compartment syndrome needing urgent surgical release.** Bleeding into closed forearm compartments strangles muscle and nerve, and only urgent fasciotomy saves the limb.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Mild bruises never turn forearms rock-tense
- C: Allergy reddens skin rather than tensing compartments
- D: Success never causes stretch-excruciating pain
**Key point:** Tense painful forearms mean compartment syndrome.
items.kp: Rock-tense painful forearms after radial access mean compartment syndrome.

items.q: A 77-year-old man needs large-bore aortic stent-grafting with 16F delivery sheaths. Both wrists pulse well and he requests radial access to walk early. Which access choice best suits this large-bore aortic case despite the request?
o: Common femoral access for its calibre and straight track
Radial access with a 16F sheath regardless
Toe artery access for comfort
No access with operation cancelled
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Common femoral access for its calibre and straight track.** Large delivery systems physically exceed radial calibre, so the femoral artery with its size and straight run stays mandatory.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Small wrists cannot pass huge sheaths
- C: Toe arteries suit nothing this large
- D: Cancelling denies life-saving repair
**Key point:** Large-bore work stays femoral.
r: Incorrect. Wrists cannot pass huge sheaths.
items.kp: Large-bore aortic work demands femoral access.

items.q: A 51-year-old man on chronic haemodialysis through a left arm fistula needs mesenteric angiography for obscure bleeding. Both groins are scarred from prior access. The trainee suggests the fistula arm for radial access. Which arm choice best protects his dialysis lifeline?
o: Avoid the fistula arm entirely and use the opposite wrist or groin
Puncture directly through the fistula for speed
Compress the fistula during the case
Tie off the fistula before angiography
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Avoid the fistula arm entirely and use the opposite wrist or groin.** Fistula arms carry infection and thrombosis risk from any extra puncture, so the lifeline arm stays untouched.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Fistula punctures clot lifelines
- C: Compressing stops dialysis flow dangerously
- D: Tying off destroys future dialysis
**Key point:** Fistula arms are never stuck electively.
items.kp: Dialysis fistula arms stay untouched by radial access.

items.q: A 60-year-old woman with Raynaud disease affecting her fingers needs uterine artery embolisation. Her radial pulses feel thready and her fingers blanch in cold. Which access decision best suits this Raynaud patient with poor wrist vessels?
o: Choose femoral access and avoid the diseased wrist arteries
Force radial access despite blanching fingers
Cool the room to test the vessels further
Prescribe ice baths before puncture
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Choose femoral access and avoid the diseased wrist arteries.** Raynaud arteries spasm and occlude readily, so diseased wrists are bypassed for the reliable femoral route.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Forcing diseased wrists invites hand ischaemia
- C: Cold triggers Raynaud attacks directly
- D: Ice worsens vasospastic disease
**Key point:** Raynaud disease rules out radial access.
items.kp: Raynaud disease with poor pulses means femoral access.

items.q: A 64-year-old man has absent radial flow on Barbeau testing with complete loss of the plethysmographic waveform on ulnar release. His ulnar pulse feels strong. Which interpretation of this absent Barbeau waveform is correct?
o: Inadequate collateral flow means avoid radial access on that side
Absent waveforms confirm excellent collaterals
The test failed so puncture blindly
Ulnar strength cancels the radial result
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Inadequate collateral flow means avoid radial access on that side.** A flat Barbeau trace proves the palm depends on the radial, so occluding it would starve the hand.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Flat traces prove dependence rather than backup
- C: Blind puncture risks hand ischaemia
- D: Strong ulnars still need waveform proof
**Key point:** Flat Barbeau traces forbid radial puncture.
r: Correct. Flat traces forbid wrist sticks.
items.kp: Absent Barbeau waveforms rule out that wrist.

items.q: A 58-year-old woman feels sharp wrist pain as the radial sheath advances despite good local anaesthetic. The operator adds verapamil with nitroglycerin through the sheath and waits. Which drug rationale best explains this vasodilator cocktail for radial pain?
o: Calcium blockade with nitric oxide relaxes arterial smooth muscle
Antibiotics sterilise the radial wall
Sedatives dissolve the catheter plastic
Steroids fuse the sheath to the skin
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Calcium blockade with nitric oxide relaxes arterial smooth muscle.** Verapamil blocks calcium entry while nitroglycerin donates nitric oxide, together unlocking spasm.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Antibiotics never relax muscle
- C: Sedatives calm patients rather than arteries
- D: Steroids never fuse plastics
**Key point:** Verapamil with nitroglycerin unlocks spasm.
items.kp: Radial cocktails pair calcium blockade with nitric oxide.

items.q: A 62-year-old man loses his radial pulse silently after transradial catheterisation but his hand stays warm with brisk capillary refill. Ulnar pulse feels bounding. Which explanation best suits this painless pulseless wrist with a warm hand?
o: Asymptomatic radial occlusion with ulnar collateral compensation
Complete hand infarction needing amputation
Successful cure of all arterial disease
Fabricated symptoms without any basis
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Asymptomatic radial occlusion with ulnar collateral compensation.** The ulnar artery carries the hand alone after silent radial clotting, leaving warmth despite the lost pulse.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Warm brisk hands are never infarcted
- C: One clot never cures arterial disease
- D: Lost pulses are objectively real
**Key point:** Silent occlusion with warm hands needs no rescue.
items.kp: Silent radial occlusion with warm hands stays untreated.

items.q: A 49-year-old woman has tortuous subclavian looping that blocks every transradial catheter from reaching the abdomen. Contrast load rises with each attempt. Which wise decision best serves this failed radial anatomy with mounting contrast?
o: Cross over to femoral access rather than forcing loops
Keep pushing until the aorta dissects
Inject contrast blindly into the arm
Discharge with the diagnosis unmade
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Cross over to femoral access rather than forcing loops.** Tortuous loops defeat wrist catheters while groin access offers a straight run, and crossover counts as judgment.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Force dissects tortuous vessels
- C: Blind injections opacify nothing useful
- D: Unmade diagnoses help nobody
**Key point:** Failed radial loops convert to femoral.
items.kp: Tortuous arm loops mean crossover to femoral.

items.q: A 71-year-old man needs complex below-knee angioplasty with long balloons and possible pedal access. The operator plans an antegrade femoral puncture. Which anatomic advantage best explains antegrade femoral choice for below-knee work?
o: Straight downhill pushability to the calf vessels
Better coronary pictures from the leg
Avoiding all radiation by distance
Cheaper balloons through groin routes
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Straight downhill pushability to the calf vessels.** Antegrade femoral sticks aim straight down the leg, transmitting push to tiny calf arteries that wrist routes cannot reach.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Legs never image coronaries
- C: Distance never avoids radiation
- D: Balloon prices ignore access sites
**Key point:** Below-knee work needs antegrade femoral push.
items.kp: Below-knee intervention favours antegrade femoral access.

items.q: A 53-year-old woman develops a small tender lump with numbness over her thumb base two weeks after radial access. Tinel tapping reproduces tingling into the thumb. Which minor radial complication does scar numbness with Tinel signs suggest?
o: Superficial radial branch irritation at the puncture scar
Carpal tunnel from typing posture
Motor neurone disease of sudden onset
Complete median nerve division
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Superficial radial branch irritation at the puncture scar.** The superficial branch runs beside the puncture where scars tether it, giving local numbness with Tinel signs.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Typing postures never follow puncture scars
- C: Neurodegeneration never starts at scars
- D: Divided nerves lose far more function
**Key point:** Scar numbness means superficial branch irritation.
items.kp: Scar numbness after radial access means branch irritation.

items.q: A 66-year-old man with a 1.6 mm radial artery on ultrasound needs visceral embolisation with 5F catheters. The operator measures carefully before deciding. Which calibre principle best guides this small radial with large catheter plans?
o: Undersized arteries need femoral access when catheters exceed safe calibre
Tiny arteries always stretch to fit anything
Catheter size never matters for access
Ultrasound measurements mislead always
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Undersized arteries need femoral access when catheters exceed safe calibre.** Sheaths wider than the artery tear and occlude it, so sub-two-millimetre radials yield to femoral for 5F work.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Arteries tear rather than stretch safely
- C: Calibre mismatch causes occlusion
- D: Ultrasound guides calibre choice well
**Key point:** Small radials yield to femoral for large catheters.
items.kp: Sub-two-millimetre radials cannot take large catheters.

items.q: A 60-year-old woman walks out two hours after transradial embolisation with a small wrist band, delighted to sit up for lunch. Her friend after femoral work stays flat till evening. Which recovery advantage best explains this early radial ambulation?
o: No groin seal to protect so sitting and walking start at once
Radial cases use no catheters at all
Wrist bands heal arteries instantly
Femoral patients enjoy bed rest more
items.exp:
**Answer: A - No groin seal to protect so sitting and walking start at once.** Wrist compression frees the hips immediately, removing the flat-rest rule that groin seals demand.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Radial cases still use full catheters
- C: Bands compress rather than heal instantly
- D: Nobody enjoys forced bed rest
**Key point:** Radial access allows immediate sitting and walking.
r: Correct. Free hips mean early walking.
items.kp: Radial access permits immediate sitting and walking.

items.q: A 57-year-old man with a high brachial bifurcation at the mid-arm needs visceral embolisation. The transradial catheter keeps entering the wrong branch at the variant takeoff. Which anatomic variant principle best explains this repeated wrong-branch entry?
o: High takeoffs create acute angles that defeat catheter torque
Variant arteries never affect catheter paths
High bifurcations improve all catheter control
Arm variants only matter for leg procedures
items.exp:
**Answer: A - High takeoffs create acute angles that defeat catheter torque.** Early branching leaves sharp turns that standard curves cannot negotiate, favouring crossover to femoral.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Variants directly steer catheters wrong
- C: Acute angles worsen rather than improve control
- D: Arm anatomy governs wrist cases
**Key point:** High brachial takeoffs defeat wrist catheters.
items.kp: High brachial bifurcations favour crossover to femoral.

items.q: A 50-year-old woman feels faint with sweating and a slow pulse as the radial needle advances. Her blood pressure dips transiently with no bleeding. Which common needle-related reflex best explains this transient bradycardia with sweating?
o: Vasovagal reaction to needling with transient vagal surge
Anaphylaxis to the steel needle metal
Massive haemorrhage from one needle pass
Stroke timed to the puncture moment
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Vasovagal reaction to needling with transient vagal surge.** Needle pain and anxiety trigger vagal slowing with sweating, recovering with lying flat and reassurance.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Steel never causes anaphylaxis
- C: Single passes rarely bleed massively
- D: Strokes never time themselves to needles
**Key point:** Needle faints are vasovagal with vagal surge.
items.kp: Needle-related faints are vasovagal reactions.

items.q: A 68-year-old man has weak bilateral radial pulses with strong brachials after years of heavy manual labour. Allen testing looks sluggish on both sides. Which bilateral access decision best suits weak wrists with sluggish collaterals?
o: Use femoral access and spare both diseased wrists
Puncture both radials simultaneously
Ignore testing and puncture blindly
Use the weaker wrist deliberately
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Use femoral access and spare both diseased wrists.** Bilateral small diseased radials with poor collaterals risk both hands, so the femoral route protects them.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Double punctures double hand risk
- C: Blind sticks on weak pulses fail often
- D: Weaker wrists occlude most readily
**Key point:** Bilateral poor wrists mean femoral access.
items.kp: Bilateral weak radials with poor collaterals mean femoral access.

items.q: A 61-year-old woman needs left gastric embolisation for bleeding and the operator works transradially from the left wrist. The trainee asks why the left wrist suits abdominal work. Which arch-anatomy advantage best explains left radial choice for visceral cases?
o: Shorter straighter run past the arch into the descending aorta
Left wrists contain larger arteries always
Right wrists cannot reach the abdomen ever
Left-sided cases need no catheters
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Shorter straighter run past the arch into the descending aorta.** The left subclavian leaves the arch nearest the descending aorta, giving wrist catheters the most direct drop into visceral branches.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Wrist sizes vary individually instead
- C: Right wrists reach abdomens with more looping
- D: Catheters remain essential either way
**Key point:** Left radial gives the straightest visceral run.
items.kp: Left radial access suits visceral work via the shortest arch run.

items.q: A 55-year-old man has his radial band removed in stages with pulse checks between loosening steps. The nurse documents return of the wrist pulse with minimal oozing. Which band-removal discipline best protects the fresh wrist seal?
o: Gradual loosening with pulse checks between steps
Ripping the band off in one pull
Tightening the band further at removal
Soaking the band off under a tap
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Gradual loosening with pulse checks between steps.** Staged release lets the seal take load progressively while pulse return confirms the artery stays open.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Single pulls tear fresh seals
- C: Tightening occludes rather than frees
- D: Soaking softens seals dangerously
**Key point:** Staged band release protects wrist seals.
items.kp: Radial bands come off gradually with pulse checks.

items.q: A 73-year-old woman with severe aortic arch tortuosity needs urgent bleeding embolisation. Both radial pulses are impalpable with calcified vessels. Which access route best serves this urgent case with impalpable wrists and tortuous arches?
o: Ultrasound-guided femoral access as the reliable urgent route
Blind wrist stabbing until blood appears
Waiting weeks for pulses to improve
Cancelling urgent bleeding control
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Ultrasound-guided femoral access as the reliable urgent route.** Impalpable wrists with tortuous arches waste urgent minutes, while ultrasound femoral sticks secure large access fast.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Blind stabs fail and destroy vessels
- C: Bleeding cannot wait weeks
- D: Cancellation lets bleeding kill
**Key point:** Urgent impalpable wrists mean ultrasound femoral.
r: Correct. Ultrasound groins save urgent cases.
items.kp: Urgent cases with poor wrists go ultrasound-guided femoral.

items.q: A 46-year-old man asks why his coronary angiogram used the wrist while his father's leg angioplasty used the groin. The registrar explains how procedure size picks access. Which size-matching principle best answers this father-son access difference?
o: Small diagnostic catheters suit wrists while large devices need groins
Access sites follow family tradition strictly
Younger patients always need groins
Fathers and sons share one artery
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Small diagnostic catheters suit wrists while large devices need groins.** Diagnostic curves pass small wrist sheaths while balloons, stents and grafts demand femoral calibre.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Tradition never picks arteries
- C: Age alone never dictates access
- D: Each patient owns separate vessels
**Key point:** Catheter size matches artery calibre.
items.kp: Access choice matches device size to artery calibre.

items.q: A 64-year-old woman develops expanding forearm swelling with blistering skin and severe pain two hours after radial sheath removal. The band site looks intact but the forearm balloons. Which band-related bleeding pattern does intact-band swelling with blistering suggest?
o: Perforation bleeding tracking up the forearm under the band
Successful haemostasis with expected swelling
Allergy to the band fabric alone
Muscle growth from the procedure
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Perforation bleeding tracking up the forearm under the band.** Small branch perforations bleed silently beneath intact bands, ballooning the forearm where pressure never reaches.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Success never balloons forearms
- C: Allergy itches rather than balloons
- D: Muscles never grow in two hours
**Key point:** Ballooning forearms mean hidden perforation bleeding.
items.kp: Ballooning forearms under intact bands mean perforation bleeding.

items.q: A 58-year-old man needs repeat transradial catheterisation one month after his first wrist case. The old puncture feels smooth with a strong pulse and normal Barbeau. Which repeat-access principle best guides this healed wrist with proven collaterals?
o: The same radial may be reused once healed with patent flow
Wrists work only once then seal forever
Repeat cases must switch limbs always
Healed arteries shatter on re-entry
items.exp:
**Answer: A - The same radial may be reused once healed with patent flow.** Healed radials with strong pulses and good collaterals accept repeat sticks, unlike freshly injured ones.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Healed wrists accept repeat puncture
- C: Limbs need not alternate when healed
- D: Healed walls hold stitches of needles
**Key point:** Healed patent radials accept repeat access.
items.kp: Healed radials with patent flow accept repeat puncture.

items.q: A 52-year-old woman undergoes left radial embolisation and the operator stands on her left with the arm abducted on a board. The radiographer positions the screen opposite. Which ergonomic setup principle best explains this left-sided room arrangement?
o: Operator, arm board and screen align along the access side
Operators must always stand on the right
Screens face away to test memory
Arm boards are purely decorative
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Operator, arm board and screen align along the access side.** Left wrist work needs the operator and imaging stacked on the left so catheters move under direct watched control.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Right-sided standing strains left access
- C: Hidden screens invite errors
- D: Boards position arms safely
**Key point:** Room setup follows the access side.
items.kp: Left radial work aligns operator and screen on the left.
